articles.title: Guest Idea: California Recently Finalized the Nation’s Strictest Plastic Packaging Rules Change Shopper Expectations
articles.summary:
In 2028, you might notice subtle changes in your grocery runs. Fruits are in cardboard...
The post Guest Idea: California Recently Finalized the Nation’s Strictest Plastic Packaging Rules Change Shopper Expectations appeared first on Earth911.
articles.content:
In 2028, you might notice subtle changes in your grocery runs. Fruits are in cardboard boxes instead of clamshell containers, takeout salads come in fiber bowls and microwaveable meals are tucked in clear or white plastic trays instead of black ones. These subtle shifts may be the result of California’s landmark packaging law, SB 54, whose finalized regulations took effect in May 2026.

Even if you don’t live in California, you will likely still see these changes. Many major manufacturers are reformulating their packaging for everyone rather than creating separate versions. And environmental groups are calling for more rigorous regulations. Oceana, NRDC and the Californians Against Waste Foundation filed suit in San Francisco Superior Court on June 2, arguing the final regulations add exclusions for large categories of plastic packaging, allow producers to claim indefinite exemptions, and fail to guard against technologies the law was designed to restrict.

What SB 54 Actually Requires

To understand why this law is so transformative, consider the scale of the problem it’s aiming to solve. For decades, plastic quietly became the default for packaging. It’s cheap, durable and lightweight. Unfortunately, its explosive growth also created a massive waste crisis.

According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the trend is taking off. Of all the municipal waste generated in the U.S., plastic waste accounted for 12.2% in 2018, a massive jump from 0.4% in 1960.

Packaging is a major part of this problem, as it’s often used once and then discarded. According to Greenprint, 36% of all manufactured plastic is used for packaging, and a staggering 85% of that material ends up in landfills. In response, California passed SB 54. Its core goals are to cut single-use plastic by 25% by 2032 and to ensure that all single-use packaging sold in the state is either recyclable or compostable.

The key mechanism driving these changes is extended producer responsibility (EPR). In simple terms, this shifts the financial burden of waste management from taxpayers and local governments to the companies that produce the packaging. This creates a powerful financial incentive for them to use less packaging, design it to be more easily recycled and avoid problematic materials.

The Packaging Materials Likely to Change First

SB 54 sets broad recyclability, compostability and source-reduction requirements that put pressure on hard-to-recycle and problematic materials. EPS food service ware is already restricted in California, while other packaging types may be redesigned, replaced or phased down as producers work toward the law’s 2032 targets.

Category 1: Polystyrene Foam

Commonly known by the brand name “Styrofoam,” expanded polystyrene (EPS) is everywhere. It’s in foam takeout containers, single-use coffee cups, coolers and the crumbly white blocks used as protective packaging.

California prohibits the sale, distribution and import of EPS food service ware. It’s mostly air, making it costly to transport, and it breaks into small pieces that contaminate other, more valuable recycled materials. Plus, research found that exposure to styrene, a key component of polystyrene, is linked to higher risks for lymphoma, leukemia and other health conditions.

The alternatives to EPS are already common. They include molded fiber containers, such as those used in egg cartons, cardboard and other paper-based clamshells, and other paper-based food service ware.

Category 2: Black and Dark-Colored Plastic Food Packaging

This refers to the black plastic used for microwaveable meal trays, the bottom of takeout sushi containers and some produce trays. The problem lies in their color.

Modern recycling facilities use near-infrared (NIR) optical sorters to identify and separate different types of plastic. As Earth911 explains, the sorting machines can’t detect the carbon black pigment used to create the dark color because it absorbs the NIR light. The sorters can’t categorize the materials, so they’re automatically rejected and sent to landfills.

In a few years, you might see clear or light-colored polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic containers replacing black food packaging. Sorters can easily identify them, and they’re among the most valuable plastics to recycle. Aluminum or fiber-based trays may also become a common sight.

Category 3: PVC Clamshells and Blister Packs

Polyvinyl chloride (PVC), also known as vinyl, is a rigid plastic often used for clear clamshells that hold berries, salads or bakery items. The blister packs that encase products like toys and batteries also include the material.

PVC packaging could face significant pressure under SB 54 because it’s a major contaminant in the PET recycling stream. Even a small amount of PVC mixed in with a bale of PET can ruin the entire batch, rendering it unusable. The additives that make the plastic flexible also pose health concerns. Research shows that PVC contains phthalates, which are associated with chronic conditions, like diabetes and infertility.

As an alternative, there’s a push for clamshells made from recycled PET (rPET). They look identical but are easier to recycle. You might also see more molded pulp containers and simple cardboard packaging.

Category 4: Oxo-Degradable Plastics

Oxo-degradable plastics are conventional plastics, like polyethylene, with special additives that cause them to break down into smaller pieces when exposed to heat or sunlight. They’re often vaguely marketed as “eco-friendly” or “degradable.”

Oxo-degradable plastics could face significant pressure under SB 54’s recyclability, compostability and anti-greenwashing goals because they’re not truly biodegradable. Instead of breaking down into harmless organic matter, they fragment into microplastics, which creates a much more pervasive and difficult-to-clean-up form of land and water pollution.

This ban is a direct strike against misleading marketing. It reinforces the point that if a product claims to be biodegradable, it must meet rigorous scientific standards.

Product Categories That Will Look Different at the Store

Beyond plastic bans, the law pushes for source reduction and improved recyclability to change the look and feel of packaging in nearly every supermarket aisle. Here are some product categories that may see the most significant changes.

1. Fresh Produce Section

Plastic clamshells stacked high with fruits, single-use plastic bags for loose greens and vegetables, and foam trays wrapped in plastic film often dominate this area. In time, those clamshells may be replaced by ventilated cardboard boxes or molded fiber punnets. The foam trays will disappear in favor of recyclable cardboard trays.

Stores will shift from single-use plastic produce bags to paper bags. Some may also market reusable mesh produce bags for purchase. Shoppers might also notice packaging-related changes in price or availability as brands and shops transition to compliant materials.

2. Prepared Foods and Deli

Deli and prepared food sections are typically a sea of clear plastic containers for items like potato salads, soups and pre-made meals. Fiber-based bowls and containers will likely replace them. They may be lined with a thin, plant-based, compostable polylactic acid (PLA) layer to handle wet foods. Lids will also transition to either compostable versions or more easily recycled plastic types.

Be aware that these fiber containers may not keep food as fresh as their airtight plastic counterparts. You can transfer leftovers into your own glass or durable plastic containers at home to maximize freshness. Expect businesses to update their packaging between 2028 to 2030.

3. Personal Care Products

Virgin plastic bottles, tubes and jars fill the health and beauty aisles. One of the first changes you’ll likely see among them is their labels, which may soon include marks like “made with X recycled plastic.”

California packaging rules already include a 25% postconsumer-material compliance option for some rigid plastic packaging containers. SB 54 adds broader pressure for covered packaging to become recyclable or compostable and meet rising recycling rate targets by 2032. While there is no have 2027 to 2032 to gradually transition their products.

More brands might offer in-store refill stations or sell smaller, concentrated pods that you can mix with water in a reusable bottle at home. As noted by experts in sustainability, a well-designed refill system reduces the need for single-use plastics entirely, which in turn conserves resources.

4. Takeout and Food Service

Getting takeout usually also means receiving assorted packaging, from foam containers to non-recyclable black plastic bowls. SB 54 pushes for standardization. Restaurants will be heavily incentivized to adopt packaging that is either widely recyclable, like aluminum foil containers, or certified as commercially compostable, such as unlined fiber containers.

This will result in clearer and more reliable disposal instructions. The goal is to eliminate the guesswork, making it obvious whether your takeout container belongs in the recycling bin, the green waste bin or the trash.

5. Online Shopping Packaging

Shipping tiny items with a ton of air pillows, bubble wrap or foam peanuts is a common practice for online shops. It keeps the parcel safe, but generates significant unnecessary waste. The law targets this “void fill.”

Expect a dramatic shift to paper-based interior packaging. This includes crumpled kraft paper, die-cut cardboard inserts and other materials that can be tossed directly into your curbside recycling bin along with the box itself. While some major retailers, such as Amazon, have already begun this transition voluntarily, the law makes it mandatory for all companies shipping products in or to California. Full compliance is expected by 2032.

The Timeline — When to Expect Changes

The massive changes SB 54 requires won’t happen all at once. The law establishes a multiyear road map for producers to adapt. Here are key deadlines to keep in mind as you watch these changes appear on local store shelves.

SB 54 Compliance Timeline: What Is Actually Required, and When Date What the Law Requires What Shoppers May Notice May 1, 2026 Permanent regulations take effect on filing. Producers had until June 1 to register with the Circular Action Alliance, register with CalRecycle as an independent producer, or claim the small producer exemption. Little visible change on shelves. Expect corporate announcements about packaging redesigns rather than redesigned packaging. January 1, 2027 Full program implementation begins. Single-use plastic packaging must fall 10% below the 2023 baseline. Producers outside an approved plan cannot sell covered materials in California. Mitigation fund payments begin. Thinner, lighter packaging and trimmed secondary packaging: fewer sleeves, window films, and oversized boxes. January 1, 2028 30% of covered single-use plastic packaging and food service ware must actually be recycled, not merely be recyclable. A shift toward materials sorting equipment can identify: clear or light-colored PET, molded fiber, aluminum, and cardboard. January 1, 2030 The recycling rate target rises to 40%. Source reduction must reach 20%. Refill stations, concentrate pods, and returnable containers move from pilot programs to routine offerings in more stores. January 1, 2032 All three final targets apply: 25% source reduction, a 65% recycling rate, and 100% of covered packaging recyclable or compostable. The full effect of the law should be visible across store shelves, with regulators deciding whether to set stricter targets. Expanded polystyrene food service ware has been prohibited in California since January 1, 2025, after the industry failed to demonstrate a 25% recycling rate. Note that CalRecycle’s final regulations are being challenged in court, so some details may change. Source: CalRecycle and the text of SB 54.

While SB 54 puts the primary responsibility on producers, you, as a consumer, have a crucial role. Being an informed shopper sends powerful market signals that can accelerate the transition to better packaging. Here’s how you can do that.

1. Identify Compliant Packaging

Look for clear labeling that indicates progress. This can include phrases like “100% recycled content” or a “how to recycle” label that gives specific disposal instructions. For items claiming to be compostable, look for an official certification logo.

Look for ASTM D6400 certification. According to the National Sanitation Foundation (NSF), this standard indicates the plastic is biodegradable and will break down under the high-heat conditions of a municipal or industrial composting facility. That means the item will not break down in your backyard compost pile or in a landfill.

Be skeptical of vague, uncertified claims like “eco-friendly,” “earth-conscious” or “biodegradable” without a specific certification logo as proof.

2. Support Brands Making Early Changes

Every purchase you make sends a data point to retailers and manufacturers. By choosing products from companies that are proactively adopting more sustainable packaging, you are casting a vote for those practices.

Many manufacturers are already publicizing their efforts to comply with and even exceed new standards. For example, Faerch, a packaging company, has already committed to producing CPET trays with at least 40% rPET. Meanwhile, massive consumer brand Unilever has publicly updated its packaging processes around a reduction, circulation and collaboration-based strategy.

3. Understand Disposal During the Transition

Remember that recyclability is local. A package might be technically recyclable, but that’s meaningless if your local facility doesn’t have the equipment or end-market to process it. Check your city or waste hauler’s website to determine the exact materials they accept for recycling.

Compostable plastic and fiber products are designed to break down in the high-heat environment of a commercial or industrial composting facility. They will not break down in a landfill or a typical backyard compost pile. If your community doesn’t offer a green waste program that accepts food service ware, these items currently belong in the trash.

4. Advocate for Better Implementation

If your community lacks robust recycling or commercial composting services, let your local representatives know that you support investment in these areas. Better infrastructure is key to reaching the 65% recycling rate goal.

State bodies like CalRecycle are required to have public comment periods as they refine the rules. You can submit comments to encourage strong enforcement and prevent industry-friendly loopholes.

The Ripple Effect — Other States Watching California

SB 54 is not an isolated event. It’s part of a growing trend of states taking legislative action on plastic waste and promoting producer responsibility.

States With Similar Legislation in Progress

Several states have either already passed or are actively considering similar EPR laws for packaging. New York is a major state to watch. It has a proposed bill that sets EPR as its core framework, signaling a similar policy direction on the East Coast.

In the Pacific Northwest, Oregon is leading with its Recycling Modernization Act. Like SB 54, it encourages manufacturers to use sustainable materials by making them financially responsible for funding improvements to the state’s recycling system. States like Colorado, Maine and Vermont have also passed their own forms of EPR for packaging.

What Interstate Coordination Means

For a company that sells products in all 50 states, managing different packaging requirements and fees for each state is a logistical and financial nightmare. It is far more efficient to design a single package that meets the strictest regulations in the country, California in this case, and then sell that same package everywhere. Because of this market reality, California’s law effectively sets the bar for the entire nation.

There’s also potential for regional harmonization. As California, Oregon and Washington all implement similar laws, a powerful “West Coast” standard may emerge. This can put even more pressure on national brands to adopt a single, high standard for their packaging.

Federal Inaction Driving State Action

In the absence of a single federal EPR framework for packaging, states are creating their own rules. This has led to the current “patchwork” of different state-level regulations. The National Conference of State Legislatures notes that California, Colorado, Maine, Maryland and Oregon have enacted packaging EPR legislation, creating a state-by-state policy landscape for producers to navigate.

The Greenwashing Concerns — What to Watch Out For

A new law means new marketing. As companies scramble to comply with SB 54, many will make bold environmental claims. Some are legitimate, but others can be misleading. This practice is known as “greenwashing.” Here’s what to watch out for so you can tell the difference.

1. Material Switching That Doesn’t Solve Problems

Be wary of companies replacing a banned material with a new one that has its own, sometimes hidden, set of environmental problems. A prime example is the confusing world of “bioplastics.”

On the surface, bioplastics sound great. They come from renewable resources like cornstarch rather than fossil fuels and are designed to break down naturally under the right conditions. However, just because a material is “plant-based” doesn’t automatically make it better. The full environmental impact of growing the crops, processing the material and what happens to it after disposal is complex.

A study revealed that some certified compostable bags actually contain more chemical additives than conventional plastic bags. They can exhibit moderate toxicity to marine plankton, proving that even “eco-friendly” alternatives need scrutiny.

2. False Equivalencies

A classic example is a paper coffee cup or soup container. It looks like paper, so it feels recyclable. However, its invisible inner plastic lining makes it a mixed material that most paper recycling facilities cannot recycle.

Some marketers might label a product as “biodegradable” to make consumers feel good about throwing it away. But nothing, not even food scraps, is designed to biodegrade in a modern, oxygen-deprived landfill. The claim is technically true in a lab but practically meaningless in the real world.

3. Third-Party Certifications That Matter

The best way to cut through confusing marketing claims is to look for logos from independent, third-party organizations. These groups have verified a product’s claims against a rigorous, scientific standard.

For any product claiming to be compostable, look for the Biodegradable Products Institute (BPI) logo. This is the gold standard in North America and proves a product will break down safely in a commercial composting facility.

For recyclability, check for the How2Recycle label. This label provides clear, honest instructions on which parts of a package are recyclable, which need to be taken to a store drop-off and which belong in the trash.

4. Questions to Ask Brands

Don’t be afraid to ask brands specific questions via social media or email. Here are a few sharp questions to get real answers:

Is this packaging accepted for recycling in the majority of curbside programs in California?

What exact percentage of post-consumer recycled content does this packaging contain?

Your package is labeled ‘compostable.’ Can you confirm it is BPI Certified to the ASTM D6400 standard?

The Long-Term Vision—What Success Looks Like

SB 54 will fundamentally redesign California’s relationship with single-use packaging. Here’s a look at what a successful circular economy looks like a decade from now with this law in effect.

2032 Targets and Beyond

For 2032, the targets are to achieve a 25% reduction in the total amount of plastic packaging sold and a 65% recycling or composting rate for all remaining packaging. Hitting a 65% recycling rate for packaging is a monumental challenge. Current recycling rates for plastics are extremely low, often in the single digits.

As experts frequently point out, even when a plastic type is recyclable, only a fraction is recyclable in actual practice. This is due to challenges in sorting, contamination from food residue and a lack of stable end-markets to turn the old plastic into new products.

The law includes provisions for regulators to set even stricter targets in the future. If California meets its 2032 goals, the next step could be pushing for even higher recycling rates or further reductions in plastic use.

Infrastructure Investments From EPR Fees

The law doubles as a funding mechanism. The EPR fees paid by producers will create a multimillion-dollar annual fund dedicated to improving the system.

A huge portion of this money will go to cities and counties to upgrade their material recovery facilities (MRFs). This means investing in better sorting equipment, like more advanced optical sorters and robotics, to capture more materials. These funds will also be used to expand access to commercial composting programs, enabling more residents to properly dispose of compostable food service ware.

Expected Behavioral Shifts

The goal is to make sustainable choices the default, easy option for consumers. Imagine subscribing to a service where restaurants serve your food in durable, stainless steel containers that are later picked up, professionally washed and reused.

For products like hand soap, cleaning supplies and shampoo, the vision is to shift away from buying a new plastic bottle every time. Instead, you’ll have a single bottle at home that you can refill from bulk bins at the grocery store or with small concentrate pods sold in paper packaging.

What This Means for a Circular Economy

In a true circular system, design eliminates waste. Products and packaging are intentionally created from the start to be easily disassembled and either recycled back into the same product or safely composted back into the earth. This is the long-term vision of SB 54. It’s a shift where producers are fully responsible for the entire life cycle of their products, keeping valuable materials in the economy and out of landfills and oceans.

Practical Shopping Guide

Small, intentional choices can make a big difference. Consider these tips on your next shopping trip.

Produce: Choose loose fruits and vegetables whenever possible and bring your own reusable mesh bags. If you need a container, look for produce in cardboard punnets or molded fiber trays instead of plastic clamshells.

Choose loose fruits and vegetables whenever possible and bring your own reusable mesh bags. If you need a container, look for produce in cardboard punnets or molded fiber trays instead of plastic clamshells. Dairy: When you have the option, choose milk in returnable glass bottles or paper cartons. Pick one large, recyclable tub over multiple single-serving cups for yogurt, cottage cheese or sour cream.

When you have the option, choose milk in returnable glass bottles or paper cartons. Pick one large, recyclable tub over multiple single-serving cups for yogurt, cottage cheese or sour cream. Meat and seafood: Visit the butcher or seafood counter and ask for your items to be wrapped in butcher paper. This avoids non-recyclable foam trays and plastic film that are common in the self-serve section.

Packaged goods: For pantry staples like sauces, beans and vegetables, prioritize glass jars and metal cans, as both have high recycling rates. For pasta, cereal and other dry goods, choose brands that use boxes made from 100% recycled cardboard.

For pasta, cereal and other dry goods, choose brands that use boxes made from 100% recycled cardboard. Personal care: The most sustainable option is often a solid bar, as it eliminates plastic packaging. If you prefer liquid products, look for brands that offer durable bottles with a clear and easy refill system.

The most sustainable option is often a solid bar, as it eliminates plastic packaging. If you prefer liquid products, look for brands that offer durable bottles with a clear and easy refill system. Cleaning products: Many brands offer cleaning products as small pods or tablets that you mix with water in a reusable spray bottle at home. This eliminates the need to ship water across the country and buy a new plastic bottle every time.

This eliminates the need to ship water across the country and buy a new plastic bottle every time. Takeout: Bring your own containers when possible and support restaurants that use compostable packaging.

The changes you see in California are a preview of a nationwide trend, with brand choices and feedback shaping how fast they happen. The transition period has already begun. Contribute to the shift by making smarter, more informed choices on your next shopping trips. Aim to reduce your overall consumption and reuse items as many times as you can before worrying about recycling.

About the Author

Rose Morrison is the managing editor of Renovated Magazine. She has over six years of experience writing about sustainability, circular economy, and better building. When not contributing to various reputable publications and advocating for environmental awareness, Rose loves being outdoors and spending time with her pets.

articles.title: As Montana warms, Missoula’s first heat map reveals hidden hotspots
articles.content:
Researchers have found that the amount of green space and shade in a neighborhood can significantly shape temperatures. On average, neighborhoods with more trees and green space — instead of impermeable surfaces like pavement — can run anywhere from 1 to 7 degrees Fahrenheit cooler. The phenomenon, which has been well studied in major urban cities, is called the “heat island effect.” But researchers have done far less work examining how those trends play out in more rural parts of the country.

Missoula, Montana, is helping fill that gap. In 2024, Climate Smart Missoula, a local nonprofit, teamed up with the city and county of Missoula and secured federal funding for a heat mapping initiative. Last summer, teams of volunteers drove countywide transects with sensors recording second-by-second measurements of temperature and humidity. Then analysts with the climate adaptation consulting firm CAPA Strategies turned the data into a now-publicly available heat map for the county. It’s the first of its kind for the state and this region of the Rockies. (Cities in Wyoming, North Dakota, and South Dakota also do not have heat maps.)

A humidity and heat sensor attached to a car window collect data to create Missoula County’s heat map.

Ellis Juhlin

The research is especially important because Missoula has historically had warm, dry summers. Temperatures in the western Montana county climb into the 80s, with occasional stretches in the 90s, before cooling off sharply after sunset. But that pattern has shifted in recent years, with hotter summers and warmer nights. The area is already experiencing more days with temperatures above 90 degrees F each year. The county’s average annual temperature is projected to increase by 4 to 5 degrees F by 2050.

The change poses particular challenges for places like Missoula, where homes, buildings, and other public infrastructure were built for cooler climates. Montana has one of the lowest rates of residential air conditioning in the country. When the heat builds, Montanans don’t have the same infrastructure as Arizonans or Texans to keep cool.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The researchers found that temperatures can vary by nearly 20 degrees across Missoula County depending on the prevalence of shade from trees and other green spaces. Susan Teitelman, with Climate Smart Missoula, said their findings mirror heat maps in other larger cities across the country.

“What we’re seeing in Missoula mimics larger cities like New York and Boston,” she said. “You see the same thing happening everywhere: Poorer, hotter neighborhoods have fewer trees; wealthier, greener neighborhoods have lower temperatures.”

Alli Kane, the county’s climate action program coordinator, said some of the results weren’t surprising. Neighborhoods like the University District or the Rattlesnake, where large, mature trees provide shade, were significantly cooler than the Northside or Westside.

“Places where we anticipated we would have heat islands were downtown Missoula, around Southgate Mall, those areas that are more urban and more built up,” Kane said.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But there were surprises, too, including how dry, brown open lands, like an empty lot in town, acted as heat islands, according to Kane. These unmanaged and undeveloped spaces tend to be a magnet for invasive species that quickly adapt to hot and dry conditions. When they’re left unwatered and not replaced with native species, they can act as heat islands, Kane said. The research showed heavily forested places like Seeley Lake and Evaro, a rural area north of the city center with dense trees, also held on to heat overnight.

“You’ll see, especially in the morning map, they are retaining heat from the day before because of that really dense canopy, and so that effect is resulting in some of our highest-recorded morning temperatures,” Kane said.

Agencies like the National Weather Service have consistently identified heat as the most deadly weather Americans experience. Research from the University of Montana published in 2024 found that for every 1 degree Celsius temperature increase, 911 calls increased correspondingly by 1 percent. Many of those calls came from rural areas with older, retired populations that are more susceptible to extreme heat.

The city and county of Missoula and Climate Smart launched a campaign called Stay Cool Missoula to build community resilience for extreme heat and attempt to prevent those deaths. Teitelman with Climate Smart Missoula pointed out that it’s critical to prepare communities for what is coming.

“Extreme heat is dangerous,” she says. “It is impacting Missoula and Montana. It’s impacting northern climates, and it’s an issue of equity.”

Teitelman leads Climate Smart’s efforts to plant trees in lower-income neighborhoods where tree cover is sparse or nonexistent. Having access to the heat map has helped her target those planting efforts. The map has been put to use in other ways too, like conversations around the proposed data center in Bonner on the banks of the Blackfoot River. That project was ultimately canceled by the property manager. But Kane said being able to showcase just how much warmer that area is, due to the amount of land cleared for industrial use, will help inform the county on future regulations and decision-making.

Missoula was one of 11 communities — including New Orleans, Memphis, Buffalo, and Moab, among others — that NOAA funded as part of a nationwide effort to map heat islands in 2025. But the work almost didn’t happen.

Like many federally funded projects related to climate change, it was targeted by the Trump administration. Kane, Teitelman, and their other partners had been awarded the grant from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Center for Collaborative Heat Monitoring Program in 2024. The money was allocated in the Inflation Reduction Act, the 2022 climate law passed by Congress. The Trump administration then terminated the funding in May 2025.

About half of the money was spent or allocated to partners before the grant’s cancellation, but Teitelman said it was a team effort to carry out the work after funds were rescinded. Climate Smart, along with the city and county of Missoula, had the staff to continue the work, but they also relied on free assistance from CAPA Strategies and other national collaborators.

“They’ve done all this pro bono work for our community and other communities. That’s just been a boon for us and communities across the U.S. who got to do this heat mapping in light of federal funding being revoked,” Teitelman said.

Kane said the lack of funding doesn’t change the reality of a warming world.

“There has been so much disruption overturned because of what’s happening at the federal level,” she said. “But I do think that our local governments and our local organizations are pretty uniquely positioned to continue to work on this, and so we’re putting everything we can behind it.”

articles.personality_title: Missoula creates Montana’s first heat map to spot hot spots and guide cooling efforts
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – As summers get hotter in Missoula, Montana, local leaders wanted to understand which neighborhoods get the hottest and why. This is important because many homes here aren’t built for extreme heat, and few have air conditioning.

**What happened** – In 2024, Climate Smart Missoula, a local nonprofit, worked with the city and county to collect temperature and humidity data across Missoula County. Volunteers drove around with sensors to record detailed heat measurements. Experts then used this data to create the first heat map for the area, showing exactly where temperatures are highest.

**Impact** – The map revealed that neighborhoods with more trees and green space are cooler by up to 7 degrees Fahrenheit. It also showed that poorer areas often have fewer trees and higher temperatures, similar to big cities. The map found surprising heat spots in dry, empty lots and even some forested areas that trap heat overnight. This gives leaders clear information to help plant trees and cool down the hottest neighborhoods.

**What's next step** – The heat map is now being used to plan tree planting in neighborhoods that need shade most. It also helps local officials make better decisions about land use and prepare for hotter summers ahead. Despite federal funding cuts, local groups and volunteers continue this work to protect residents from rising heat.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Missoula’s new heat map reveals hidden hot spots and guides local efforts to cool neighborhoods and prepare for a warmer future.
articles.personality_title_fr: Missoula crée la première carte thermique du Montana pour identifier les zones chaudes et guider les efforts de refroidissement
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Alors que les étés deviennent plus chauds à Missoula, Montana, les responsables locaux ont voulu comprendre quels quartiers sont les plus chauds et pourquoi. C’est important car beaucoup de maisons ici ne sont pas conçues pour la chaleur extrême et peu ont la climatisation.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2024, Climate Smart Missoula, une association locale, a travaillé avec la ville et le comté pour collecter des données de température et d’humidité dans tout le comté. Des bénévoles ont parcouru la région avec des capteurs pour enregistrer des mesures précises. Des experts ont ensuite utilisé ces données pour créer la première carte thermique de la région, montrant où les températures sont les plus élevées.

**Impact** – La carte a révélé que les quartiers avec plus d’arbres et d’espaces verts sont jusqu’à 7 degrés Fahrenheit plus frais. Elle a aussi montré que les quartiers plus pauvres ont souvent moins d’arbres et des températures plus élevées, comme dans les grandes villes. La carte a trouvé des zones chaudes surprenantes dans des terrains secs et vides, ainsi que dans des forêts qui retiennent la chaleur la nuit. Cela donne aux responsables des informations claires pour planter des arbres et rafraîchir les quartiers les plus chauds.

**Prochaine étape** – La carte thermique est maintenant utilisée pour planifier la plantation d’arbres dans les quartiers qui ont le plus besoin d’ombre. Elle aide aussi les autorités locales à mieux gérer l’aménagement du territoire et à se préparer à des étés plus chauds. Malgré la réduction des financements fédéraux, les groupes locaux et les bénévoles poursuivent ce travail pour protéger les habitants.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La nouvelle carte thermique de Missoula révèle les zones chaudes cachées et guide les actions locales pour rafraîchir les quartiers et se préparer à un avenir plus chaud.
articles.personality_title_es: Missoula crea el primer mapa de calor de Montana para identificar zonas calientes y guiar esfuerzos de enfriamiento
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – A medida que los veranos se vuelven más calurosos en Missoula, Montana, los líderes locales quisieron entender qué vecindarios son los más calientes y por qué. Esto es importante porque muchas casas aquí no están diseñadas para el calor extremo y pocas tienen aire acondicionado.

**Qué pasó** – En 2024, Climate Smart Missoula, una organización local sin fines de lucro, trabajó con la ciudad y el condado para recoger datos de temperatura y humedad en todo el condado de Missoula. Voluntarios recorrieron la zona con sensores para registrar mediciones detalladas. Luego, expertos usaron esos datos para crear el primer mapa de calor de la región, mostrando dónde están las temperaturas más altas.

**Impacto** – El mapa reveló que los vecindarios con más árboles y espacios verdes son hasta 7 grados Fahrenheit más frescos. También mostró que las áreas más pobres suelen tener menos árboles y temperaturas más altas, como en las grandes ciudades. El mapa encontró puntos calientes sorprendentes en lotes secos y vacíos, y en zonas boscosas que retienen el calor durante la noche. Esto da a los líderes información clara para plantar árboles y enfriar los vecindarios más calientes.

**Próximo paso** – El mapa de calor ahora se usa para planificar la plantación de árboles en las áreas que más necesitan sombra. También ayuda a los funcionarios locales a tomar mejores decisiones sobre el uso del suelo y a prepararse para veranos más calurosos. A pesar de los recortes de fondos federales, los grupos locales y voluntarios continúan este trabajo para proteger a los residentes del aumento del calor.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El nuevo mapa de calor de Missoula revela puntos calientes ocultos y guía los esfuerzos locales para enfriar vecindarios y prepararse para un futuro más cálido.

articles.title: Hidden moth population found after 70 years
articles.summary: Dr Dave Wainwright describes the discovery as one of the highlights of his career.
articles.content:
A hidden population of one of England's rarest moths has been found at a site where it had not been seen for more than 70 years.

Head of conservation at Butterfly Conservation Dr Dave Wainwright has spent his career searching for the dark bordered beauty and said he felt an "overwhelming feeling of relief" when they were found at Wallington estate, in Northumberland.

For decades, the only site where the moth was found in England was at Strensall Common, in Yorkshire, but the population there has been in decline due to climate change and a wildfire.

The discovery has given conservationists new hope for the species and opened up the possibilities of where more can be found.

Once widespread across northern England and Scotland, habitat loss has caused significant decline in the dark bordered beauty.

The custard-and-chocolate-coloured moth was found at the National Trust site previously but had not been seen since 1952.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a hidden population of one of England's rarest moths after 70 years represents a significant conservation success. It offers hope for the species' survival and highlights the positive impact of conservation efforts against habitat loss and climate change. The story is focused, detailed, and has meaningful implications for biodiversity and environmental preservation.
articles.personality_title: Rare moth rediscovered in England after 70 years
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The dark bordered beauty is one of England's rarest moths. It was once common across northern England and Scotland but has become very rare because its natural homes have disappeared. For many years, it was only found at one place in England, Strensall Common in Yorkshire, but even there the moth’s numbers have dropped because of climate change and a wildfire.

**What happened** – Dr Dave Wainwright, head of conservation at Butterfly Conservation, and his team found a hidden group of these moths at Wallington estate in Northumberland. This is the first time the moth has been seen there since 1952. Dr Wainwright called this discovery one of the best moments of his career and said he felt a strong relief when the moths were found.

**Impact** – This rediscovery is important because it shows the dark bordered beauty still survives outside its last known home. It gives hope that the moth can be protected and that there might be more hidden populations. Finding the moth again also helps experts learn where to look and how to save it from disappearing completely.

**What's next step** – Conservationists will study the Wallington population to understand what it needs to survive. They will also search other similar places to find more groups of the moth. Protecting these habitats will be important to stop the moth from disappearing again.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After 70 years, a rare moth thought nearly lost has been found again, offering new hope for its future in England.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une rare mite redécouverte en Angleterre après 70 ans
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La beauté à bordure sombre est l'une des mites les plus rares d'Angleterre. **Impact** – Cette redécouverte est importante car elle montre que la beauté à bordure sombre survit encore en dehors de son dernier habitat connu. Cela donne de l'espoir pour la protection de la mite et suggère qu'il pourrait y avoir d'autres populations cachées. **Message clé en une phrase** – Après 70 ans, une rare mite presque disparue a été retrouvée, offrant un nouvel espoir pour son avenir en Angleterre.
articles.personality_title_es: Raro polilla redescubierta en Inglaterra después de 70 años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La belleza de borde oscuro es una de las polillas más raras de Inglaterra. Antes era común en el norte de Inglaterra y Escocia, pero ahora es muy rara porque sus hogares naturales han desaparecido. Durante muchos años, solo se encontraba en un lugar en Inglaterra, Strensall Common en Yorkshire, pero allí su número ha disminuido por el cambio climático y un incendio.

Es la primera vez que se ve esta polilla allí desde 1952. El Dr. Wainwright dijo que fue uno de los mejores momentos de su carrera y sintió un gran alivio.

Da esperanza para proteger la polilla y sugiere que puede haber más grupos escondidos. Encontrar la polilla de nuevo también ayuda a los expertos a saber dónde buscar y cómo salvarla.

**Próximo paso** – Los conservacionistas estudiarán la población de Wallington para entender qué necesita para sobrevivir. También buscarán en otros lugares similares para encontrar más grupos. Proteger estos hábitats será clave para evitar que la polilla desaparezca otra vez.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Después de 70 años, una polilla rara casi perdida ha sido encontrada de nuevo, dando nueva esperanza para su futuro en Inglaterra.

articles.title: 'Squashed poo' a sign of water voles' success
articles.summary: Signs suggest the water vole population on the Hogsmill River in Surrey has been reestablished.
articles.content:
"I've never been so excited to see a poo," says urban rewilding officer Pia Trevelyan-Ashby.

She holds out a small Tic Tac-shaped dropping from a water vole and smiles. "This is what success looks like."

She has been on the hunt for evidence of the water vole population in the Hogsmill River in Surrey.

One year ago, South East Rivers Trust and environmental organisation Citizen Zoo released 42 water voles into the chalk stream.

Now, all the signs point to a population of water voles that has not only survived the winter, but is thriving.
articles.reasoning: The article reports the successful reestablishment and thriving of a water vole population in a local river, indicating positive progress in wildlife conservation and urban rewilding efforts with tangible environmental benefits.
articles.personality_title: Water voles thrive again on Surrey’s Hogsmill River
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Water voles are small animals that live near rivers and streams. They have been disappearing in many places because of changes to their homes and predators.

**What happened** – In Surrey, England, 42 water voles were released into the Hogsmill River one year ago by two groups working to help nature: South East Rivers Trust and Citizen Zoo. Recently, an officer named Pia Trevelyan-Ashby found signs that the water voles are not just surviving but doing well. She even found their droppings, which show the animals are living happily in the area.

**Impact** – This is important because water voles are a key part of river ecosystems. Their return means the river environment is healthy enough to support wildlife again. It also shows that efforts to bring back animals to cities and towns can work, helping nature and people live together better.

**What’s next step** – The groups will continue to watch the water voles to make sure their numbers keep growing. They might also try to help other places bring back water voles or similar animals to improve local environments.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Careful efforts have helped water voles successfully return and thrive in the Hogsmill River, showing the power of nature restoration in cities.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les campagnols d'eau revivent sur la rivière Hogsmill dans le Surrey
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les campagnols d'eau sont de petits animaux qui vivent près des rivières et des ruisseaux. Ils ont disparu dans de nombreux endroits à cause des changements de leur habitat et des prédateurs.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Dans le Surrey, en Angleterre, 42 campagnols d'eau ont été relâchés dans la rivière Hogsmill il y a un an par deux groupes qui travaillent pour aider la nature : South East Rivers Trust et Citizen Zoo. Récemment, une responsable appelée Pia Trevelyan-Ashby a trouvé des signes montrant que les campagnols d'eau ne se contentent pas de survivre, mais qu'ils se portent bien. Elle a même trouvé leurs crottes, preuve que les animaux vivent heureux dans la région.

**Impact** – C’est important parce que les campagnols d'eau jouent un rôle clé dans les écosystèmes des rivières. Leur retour signifie que l’environnement de la rivière est suffisamment sain pour soutenir la faune à nouveau. Cela montre aussi que les efforts pour ramener les animaux en ville peuvent réussir, aidant la nature et les humains à mieux vivre ensemble.

**Prochaine étape** – Les groupes vont continuer à surveiller les campagnols d'eau pour s’assurer que leur nombre augmente. Ils pourraient aussi essayer d’aider d’autres endroits à faire revenir les campagnols d'eau ou des animaux similaires pour améliorer les environnements locaux.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des efforts précis ont permis aux campagnols d'eau de revenir et de prospérer dans la rivière Hogsmill, montrant la force de la restauration de la nature en milieu urbain.
articles.personality_title_es: Los topillos de agua prosperan nuevamente en el río Hogsmill en Surrey
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los topillos de agua son pequeños animales que viven cerca de ríos y arroyos. Han desaparecido en muchos lugares debido a cambios en su hábitat y a depredadores.

**Qué pasó** – En Surrey, Inglaterra, 42 topillos de agua fueron liberados en el río Hogsmill hace un año por dos grupos que trabajan para ayudar a la naturaleza: South East Rivers Trust y Citizen Zoo. Recientemente, una oficial llamada Pia Trevelyan-Ashby encontró señales de que los topillos de agua no solo están sobreviviendo, sino que están prosperando. Incluso encontró sus excrementos, que muestran que los animales viven felices en la zona.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque los topillos de agua son una parte clave de los ecosistemas de los ríos. Su regreso significa que el ambiente del río es lo suficientemente saludable para apoyar la vida silvestre otra vez. También muestra que los esfuerzos para traer animales de vuelta a las ciudades pueden funcionar, ayudando a que la naturaleza y las personas vivan mejor juntas.

**Próximo paso** – Los grupos seguirán observando a los topillos de agua para asegurarse de que su número siga creciendo. También podrían intentar ayudar a otros lugares a traer de vuelta a los topillos de agua o animales similares para mejorar los ambientes locales.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Esfuerzos cuidadosos han ayudado a que los topillos de agua regresen y prosperen en el río Hogsmill, mostrando el poder de la restauración natural en las ciudades.
articles.image_prompt: A warm, detailed painting of a gently flowing chalk stream with small, rounded water vole droppings shaped like tiny Tic Tacs scattered along the riverbank, alongside subtle silhouettes of water voles peeking from lush riverbank burrows, all rendered in soft, natural earth tones and greens.
